title: South Africa Debate Intensifies Over Ballot Paper Complexity and Electoral Thresholds
text: South Africa Debate Intensifies Over Ballot Paper Complexity and Electoral Thresholds South Africa's recent local government elections have sparked controversy over the large number of political parties on ballot papers, with critics arguing that smaller parties complicate voting and coalition formation. Prominent figures and analysts are calling for the implementation of electoral thresholds, such as a 1% or 5% vote requirement, to simplify the democratic process and reduce administrative burdens, while supporters defend the current system as essential for democratic representation. Are smaller political parties an important part of democracy, or simply cluttering elections, fragmenting votes and making coalition governments difficult to manage? Picture: Michel BegaSouth Africa’s enormous ballot papers have again ignited debate about whether smaller political parties are an important part of democracy, or simply cluttering elections, fragmenting votes and making coalition governments difficult to manage. With dozens of parties contesting the local government elections this week, political analysts and politicians are divided over whether tougher entry requirements and electoral thresholds could simplify elections without undermining democratic rights.“I would personally support a five percent threshold. We have so many political parties and candidates that the system has become unnecessarily complicated,” he said. He added that crowded ballot papers may confuse voters, while the number of participating parties place additional pressure on election administration.“The more parties you have, the greater the possibility of mistakes. It complicates the entire process, from voting to counting, and creates additional problems for the IEC,” he said. He asked whether parties attracting less than one percent of the vote justified the additional complexity.“People can argue this is democracy, but even democracy needs certain parameters. We could simplify the process without making any real difference to the outcome,” he said. DA member of the Gauteng provincial legislature and Ekurhuleni election campaign manager Mike Waters said reform is necessary.“The size of those ballot papers was ridiculous. We need electoral reform that reduces the number of parties contesting elections and, ultimately, winning seats,” he said.“If there were a threshold of one or two percent, many of these parties would simply not contest because they know they have little chance of winning a seat,” he said. Waters cited Ekurhuleni, where he said seven parties each secured a single council seat in the previous election.“Together they held the council hostage. Voters want stability and we need an electoral system that allows serious parties to govern without being held hostage by smaller parties,” he said. Though thresholds could discourage smaller parties from contesting elections, they would not automatically shorten ballot papers.However, ActionSA’s Michael Basch said that restricting smaller parties could come at a democratic cost.“The strength of our democracy is that we are open to independent candidates and smaller parties. It gives voters a wider choice and prevents us from becoming a political system dominated by just two parties,” he said. Basch said many smaller parties would disappear naturally after failing to secure seats, particularly once the financial realities of running a political organisation became apparent.“Campaigning is difficult and expensive. Many of these smaller parties will disappear once they realise what it takes to sustain a political organisation. Over time, the system will naturally settle,” he said. Basch said declining voter turnout presented a greater danger than the number of parties contesting elections.“Even if a smaller party attracts only 10, 20 or 30 votes, those could be people who would otherwise never have voted. The real danger is when people stop participating, because that makes it easier for a different party to secure a majority,” he said. Another political analyst, who consults to a major political party, proposes a 2% threshold with higher election deposits.“There should be a threshold for political parties contesting a municipality. If they fail to reach that threshold, they should forfeit their deposit. Independent ward candidates should be treated differently, because they are true neighbourhood representatives and not party animals” he said.
